item.title: Septima: A Witch's Trial
item.description:
Hello everyone!

Today I want to present you a witch game, Septima. Let’s brew some potions and save witches from the trials!

Game Overview

Septima is a 2023 release for 1–4 players, ages 12+, with a playtime of 50–100 minutes. It was designed by Robin Hegedűs, illustrated by Villő Farkas (with character art by Barbara Bernát), and published by Mindclash Games.

Theme

In Septima, you represent a witch who has come to Noctenburg to prove you’re worthy of becoming the next Septima, the leader of all witches. She is the wisest and most knowledgeable among them, and now that her time is coming to an end, witches from all over the world have gathered at Noctenburg to become her successor.

You’ll prove your worth by collecting herbs, brewing potions, healing the townsfolk, mastering charms, and rescuing your sisters and brothers from the trials. But be careful: raise too much suspicion among the townsfolk, and you’ll see the witches of your coven sent to trial instead.

How to Win

The player with the most Wisdom wins. You’ll collect Wisdom throughout the game (and lose some too), then gain more at the end by fulfilling your objectives, and mostly by scoring points from the patients you’ve treated.

Gameplay

Septima is a fully competitive game where players can still work together to boost their powers.

A game of Septima is played over a single year, made up of 4 Seasons: Autumn, Winter, Spring, and Summer. Each Season is made up of 5 Moon Phases (rounds). In each Moon Phase, you select one card from your hand to play. Every card has two effects: one that’s always resolved, and a second one that also triggers if another player plays the same card, or if it matches the Septima’s own action. All cards are revealed simultaneously, then resolved in player order.

Your possible actions include moving, collecting resources (only the Ingredients matching the current Moon Phase are available), brewing potions, treating patients, and sending Loyal Citizens to the Crowd or to a Trial Chamber.

A Trial takes place at the end of every Season. Each Trial process can involve up to 2 Trial Chambers: the First Trial Chamber always has a witch, drawn randomly from the witch stack, and is always resolved. The Second Trial Chamber only goes to trial if it has accumulated 1 or more witches from players raising too much suspicion and getting caught by the Hunters, and even if several witches have piled up there, only the one on top is put on trial.

For each Trial, all Loyal Citizens from the Crowd go into the bag, plus one Angry Citizen per suspicion level shown on each player’s board. These are drawn one by one to fill the Trial Chamber. If Loyal Citizens outnumber Angry Citizens, the player with the most Loyal Citizens in that Chamber brings the witch into their coven and scores points.

Components

The deluxe version, the one I have, comes with a really good insert that keeps everything sorted and makes setup much easier. The retail version doesn’t include this insert, so setup can take noticeably longer, worth knowing before you decide which edition to get. The meeples are lovely and the resources are a nice touch (both come in the retail version too). Card quality is excellent, and the game overall is simply beautiful. The illustrations pull you straight into the witches’ world, and the purple palette suits the theme perfectly.

Solo Mode

The solo mode was designed by Dávid Turczi. You play against an automa: the Black Widow. She doesn’t move a witch on the board but instead controls 3 spider pawns. Each round, after you choose your action, you roll a die to determine which of her 3 available action cards she takes, either one of the two face-up cards or the top face-down one. You can manipulate this choice using specific cards available to you.

The Black Widow has her own board where she tracks the witches she’s rescued, her suspicion level, and patients healed. If your action matches one of the Septima tokens (or hers), your suspicion still rises the same way as in a multiplayer game. If you’re playing with the full rules, instead of advancing on the Ritual track, the Black Widow’s Ritual action discards all the Spells from the bottom row of the Spell display.

Each round, the Black Widow moves her spiders to threaten spaces on the board: you lose 1 point if a spider ends on a space adjacent to you (or if you end your turn adjacent to her), and 5 points if a spider lands on your exact space. She also participates in Trials the same way you do.

Scoring works a bit differently in solo mode. First, don’t count the Wisdom from your Book of Divinations’ 4 objectives. Add the Wisdom you collected during the game, Wisdom from your Loyal Citizens on the Crowd or in Trial Chambers (3 Wisdom for 3 or 4 citizens, 7 Wisdom for 5 or 6), Wisdom for the highest level reached on each patient track, and an additional 6 Wisdom for each level that all three patient tracks have reached (so reaching level 2 on all three nets you 2 × 6 = 12 extra Wisdom, not just a flat one-time bonus). You also score 1 Wisdom per Good Luck Charm and 1 point per remaining potion, and 1 Wisdom for each pair of ingredients and crystals.

Then you lose Wisdom: 3 or 7 Wisdom if the Black Widow has 3/4 or 5/6 Cursed Citizens (her own equivalent of Loyal Citizens), and for each patient track, you lose Wisdom equal to the highest level reached, plus an additional 6 Wisdom for each level she’s reached on all three tracks, following the same logic as the gain side.

Winning isn’t about comparing a final Wisdom score, it comes down to completing at least 5 of 8 “Tribulations.” Four of them come from meeting your Book of Divinations objectives (no coven witches required here, unlike multiplayer), the fifth is having 4 witches in your coven, the sixth is limiting the Black Widow to 3 or fewer witches in hers, the seventh is reaching the top ribbon on the Ritual track, and the eighth is finishing with at least 42 Wisdom after all scoring. Complete 4 or fewer, and the Black Widow becomes the new Septima. Complete 5 or more, and you do.

My Experience

I’ve played Septima 3 times so far, always with the full rules and no expansions.

I really enjoyed my plays, even though I felt completely lost at the start, especially with the Black Widow’s actions. After 2 turns, though, I realised it wasn’t nearly as complicated as it first seemed. Out of my 3 plays, I’ve won 1 and lost 2. Funnily enough, winning that first game made me a little too confident going into my most recent play, where I got caught by the spiders again and again and had a hard time shaking them off. Turns out Septima rewards reflection, not swagger! 😅

Setting up the deluxe version isn’t complicated at all, the insert genuinely makes a difference, and setup itself is a pleasure: seeing all the board details and the quality of the tokens come together is part of the fun. The rulebook is well written, with helpful examples for the trickier rules. I’d have loved a quick-reference card summarising the Black Widow’s turn, though.

Beyond that, I had a really good time. The spiders are annoying in the best way, and you constantly have to weigh whether to match with another player or the Septima, since that raises your suspicion and risks getting caught by the Hunters, landing one of your witches in a trial. I really like this mechanic of potentiating your action through matching with your opponents’ choices, it adds a great layer of tension to every round.

I particularly appreciated how the Moon Phase controls resource production: only the Ingredients tied to that specific Moon are available, which is very thematic and makes you plan ahead and think carefully about when to go for which resources.

With only 5 actions per Season, it can genuinely feel tight. There were plenty of turns where I wanted to collect, brew a potion, heal a patient, and send a Loyal Citizen to the Crowd or a Trial Chamber, all while also needing to move, and sometimes adjusting my plan entirely just to avoid matching with the Septima or the Black Widow. It’s easy to feel overwhelmed wanting to do everything at once, and simply not being able to.

My favourite potion is the one that lets you move, it makes managing your position on the board so much easier.

In solo mode, the game becomes a real puzzle. I never found it boring, I could genuinely lose myself in it. I haven’t tested the Shapeshifting & Omens expansion yet, but I’m keen to try it. As for the full ruleset itself, I think it makes the most sense for players already experienced with board games, there’s more to think about, but not more complexity than you can handle.

I haven’t played in multiplayer yet, but I expect the game will shine even more there, with matching actions and negotiation between players happening far more often.

My Rating

Note: 8/10

Septima earns this score for its striking production, a theme that comes through in every mechanic, and the constant tension of deciding whether to risk matching an opponent’s move. It’s a game that rewards patience and reflection over confidence.

Final Thoughts

Septima brings its theme, artwork, and mechanics together in a way that feels genuinely cohesive, brewing potions, healing patients, and managing suspicion all pull in the same direction, and every round has real weight to it. Whether you’re up against the Black Widow solo or negotiating your way through a coven of rivals, there’s plenty here to sink your teeth into. If you enjoy strong theming and clever player interaction, Septima deserves a spot on your table.

Your Turn

Have you played Septima, solo or with a coven of friends? I’d love to hear how your trials went. Come share your comments on Mastodon and Facebook.

item.title: Rise of a Kingdom: My Time with Era of Kingdoms
item.description:
Hello everyone!

Today I’m taking you to the Era of Kingdoms, where you’ll build your domain, attract people to it, and go head to head with rival kingdoms. Who will come out on top as the strongest realm? Let’s find out how to play!

Game Overview

Era of Kingdoms is a 2019 release for 1 to 4 players, ages 14+, with a playtime of 30 to 45 minutes. It was designed by Michael Erisman and illustrated by Jeff Porter and published by KC Games.

Theme

In Era of Kingdoms, you compete to bring your kingdom from the dark ages into the age of enlightenment. You’ll cultivate your lands, build up your military strength and defences, and strike up trades along the way. You’ll also attract people to populate your lands and help carry you to victory.

Gameplay

The rules are simple. The game is played in turns, and each turn gives you 3 actions to spend. You can use them to play a card from your hand, draw a basic card from the deck, or draft a basic card from the Trade Route board if you’re using that expansion. On top of that, at no action cost and with no limit, you can remove cards from your board (except plague cards) and use a Riches card to borrow resources from another player, once per turn.

Every card has resource requirements it needs met before it can be played, drawn from the lands and people already in your kingdom. Once you have 3 level 2 cards in play, you place your town centre card to show your kingdom is growing. Get 3 level 3 cards on the table and you can flip your card over to the castle side, the highest kingdom level there is.

Upgrading is genuinely worth chasing, not just for show. Once you reach town centre level, you can draw or draft 1 card from the intermediate deck each turn on top of your basic cards. Reach castle level and you can draw or draft 1 advanced card and 2 intermediate cards each turn. This is where the game really opens up, since better cards mean better options.

The game ends when the Age of Enlightenment card appears, which happens once players start drawing from the advanced deck. Whoever draws it gets one final point, and everyone gets one last turn to grab as many Victory Points as they can before scores are tallied.

How to Win

The winner is whoever ends the game with the most Victory Points. You earn these mainly through era 2 and era 3 cards, which can be land cards, people cards, or “Play Immediately” cards. The Age of Enlightenment card, which signals the last turn of the game, also gives one point to whoever draws it.

Components

The game is packed with cards, along with a handful of boards. You’ll find components for the base game plus all 3 mini expansions inside the box, with no tokens to speak of. The card quality is good, and the illustrations are beautiful and thematic throughout. The boards match that same quality, nicely illustrated too.

The box cover fits the theme with its dark colours echoing that journey from the dark ages to enlightenment, but it’s also a bit faded, which means it can easily get lost on a shelf next to other games. The rulebook, on the other hand, is well explained, with a good typography size that’s easy to read without straining.

Setup

Setup is quick. Shuffle the 3 card decks (basic, intermediate, and advanced), then place the Enlightenment card at a set position from the top: 9 cards for a 2 player game, 11 for 3 players, or 13 for 4 players. Each player sets up their own board with 3 Riches cards, 1 town centre card, and 1 player turn guide, then draws 5 basic cards.

If you’re already familiar with deck builders, I’d recommend adding the Trade Route expansion straight away, solo or multiplayer. This adds a river of cards: for setup, place 6 basic cards, 3 intermediate, and 1 advanced face up on the Trade Route board.

Solo Mode

The solo opponent, the Shadow Kingdom, is refreshingly easy to manage. Each turn, the Shadow Kingdom draws cards based on your own kingdom’s progression, not its own, so the better you’re doing, the more it draws too. These cards go straight into its play area. At the end of the game, you total up both scores and compare. The trick is staying attentive to what the Shadow Kingdom is collecting, so you can try to optimise your own cards along the way.

My Experience

I’ve played Era of Kingdoms solo 3 times so far. My first game was the pure base game, and the next two included the Trade Route mini expansion, which for me is a must have.

  • Game 1: 21 vs the Shadow Kingdom’s 31 (Shadow Kingdom won)
  • Game 2: 27 vs the Shadow Kingdom’s 14 (I won!)
  • Game 3: 26 vs the Shadow Kingdom’s 32 (Shadow Kingdom won)

One thing that stood out in my first game was having a good people card in hand but my person tiles already full. In that moment I had to decide whether the new card was worth discarding an existing one for, or whether I was better off sticking with what I had. The start of the game can also be a bit tricky solo, since you sometimes need a specific land card to build on and it can be hard to find in the deck. Luckily the basic deck has a lot of duplicates, so it’s not too bad, but you can still struggle a little, and changing direction isn’t always possible depending on what’s in your hand.

As for the Trade Route expansion, playing without it didn’t feel like real deck building to me, since there’s no card river. You’re stuck with whatever random cards you draw, with no control at all. That’s fine for newer players, but for anyone with more deck building experience under their belt, it’s not quite satisfying enough. Adding the Trade Route brings back that deck building feel and really rounds out the game.

Most cards don’t have a lot of text or effects beyond their base function, aside from event cards and “Play Immediately” cards, which I really appreciated. It keeps things simple to track, and the main thing to manage is resources, whether for building stronger cards or boosting attack and defence. When events call for a fight, it’s simple to resolve too, just compare attack and defence points. That lack of clutter makes this a great pick for introducing new players to deck building without extra rules to juggle.

All three plays were enjoyable. This was a game I’d never even heard of before, and I’m glad I got the chance to put it on the table and try it out. I’ll definitely be bringing it to the group to see how it plays with others.

My Rating

Note: 7/10

There are other deck builders I enjoy more, like Ascension, Legendary Encounters: Alien, and Harry Potter: Hogwarts Battle. Those are more complete and complex games. But Era of Kingdoms is a lovely way to introduce new players to deck building, and it’s worth it for the illustrations alone.

Final Thoughts

It’s still an enjoyable game that deserves to be better known. It’s a solid option for anyone who enjoys lite deck building with beautiful illustrations.

Your Turn

Have you played Era of Kingdoms, or do you have another lite deck builder with gorgeous art that deserves more love? Come share them on Mastodon and *Facebook

item.title: June 2026 Plays
item.description:
Hello everyone!

How was your June? Mine was good, with a lot of sun, beach, and of course, games. I played 22 games this month, which is really good for me. Looking back at my plans from last month, I managed to play almost everything I wanted: Minos, Septima, and Hogwarts Battle. Unconscious Mind didn’t make it to the table this time, let’s see if I can fix that in July. So, let’s take a tour of what June brought.

June 2026 by Numbers

  • 22 plays (vs. 24 in May)
  • 12 different games
  • 2 new games to me
  • Most played: Harry Potter: Hogwarts Battle

New Games

Minos: Dawn of the Bronze Age

Designed by Stan Kordonskiy, published by Board&Dice.

In Minos, you’re a member of one of the illustrious Minoan clans, competing to become the ultimate leader of your people. You’ll select actions through dice placement, and the way it works is clever: each action row favours the leftmost die, so if another player places a die with a lower value on the same row, your die slides to the right. You need to balance selecting dice that let you progress on the influence tracks (summing 9 on a single colour, or combining with grey dice) against grabbing the strongest actions with lower values. And that’s only part of it, you’ll also play cards for extra actions or place them on your palace to score at the end, plus area control with movement across a map as your people spread and build palaces, towers, and farms.

The game is huge, you’ll need a big table and a lot of space, and I was disappointed there’s no insert given how much material comes in the box. I’ve only played once so far, and honestly, the first play felt confusing, I didn’t really know how to combo or what to prioritise. I think I started to understand by the end. For now I’ll rate it 7/10, but that will probably change after a few more plays.

7 Wonders Architects

Designed by Antoine Bauza, published by Repos Production.

I finally got 7 Wonders Architects to the table, at 2 players. I’d wanted to try it for a while, and now it’s done. At that count, the game doesn’t quite shine, and you can feel it from the first round. It’s an easy game, ideal for introducing new people to the hobby, and the production is excellent, with the monuments beautifully represented. It plays very similarly to 7 Wonders Duel, which I’ve played several times: cards bring you resources, science, points, and shields. When you complete part of your monument, you discard the resource cards used, unlike 7 Wonders, where resources are never discarded. If a war is triggered, you compare shields, and the player with the most wins victory points (some shield cards get discarded too). With science, collecting two matching symbols or three different ones lets you take a bonus, and again those cards are discarded. You draft from the central deck, your own personal deck, and the decks on either side of you.

At a higher player count I think this would be a lot more fun, at 2 players it’s still fine and entertaining, but you’ll quickly notice what could be better, mainly that the cards don’t turn over quickly enough. I’ll give it 6/10.

Preferred Game of the Month

It’s a Wonderful World

Designed by Frédéric Guérard, published by La Boîte de Jeu.

It’s probably no surprise by now that It’s a Wonderful World is my favourite game from everything I played this month. I love this game, and I’ve already written a full review, which you can find here. It’s a 10/10 for me: quick, with easy rules, but it makes you think carefully about which cards to build or discard to optimise your production engine and points. It plays beautifully both solo and multiplayer, which is part of why it’s one of my beloved games. I’m currently working through the Leisure & Decadence campaign expansion and have already finished War or Peace. I’ll probably write a review of both soon, along with the third expansion, Corruption & Ascension.

Harry Potter: Hogwarts Battle

Designed by Forrest-Pruzan Creative, Kami Mandell, and Andrew Wolf, published by The Op.

Hogwarts Battle is a cooperative game for 2-4 players that also works really well solo, I usually play two hands, managing two characters. The game progresses through the years at Hogwarts: in the base box you can be Harry, Hermione, Ron, or Neville, fighting off the dark arts enemies. The rules evolve as you unlock material by opening each year’s box, adding new rules, enemies, and cards. It’s a deckbuilder, though with one downside for me: you can’t remove cards from your hand to improve your deck, so you end up carrying powerless cards throughout. Even though the game can be played in a campaign style, it isn’t a true campaign, you can pick different characters each time since you don’t carry improvements between plays, always starting fresh each year. That’s another thing I’d love to see change: carrying some knowledge from game to game. Still, for Harry Potter fans this game is a real treat, all the characters from the story are here, and the experience is lovely. Plays get longer as you advance through the years, but the enjoyment stays. I’ll give it a 7/10, it loses points on those gameplay quirks, but the theme is excellent and I’d happily come back to it again and again.

Other Notable Games

Septima (designed by Robin Hegedűs, published by Mindclash Games) — A witchcraft game where you lead a coven, avoiding the hunters while gaining enough wisdom to become the next Septima. Each round you play a card with an action, and if you match the action with another player or the Septima, you can execute a more powerful version, at the cost of raising suspicion. I played solo, and the tension of avoiding the Black Widow’s spiders (which cost you wisdom) never really lets up. It felt a touch repetitive, but the production is fantastic, with real table presence. 7.5/10.

Nautilion (designed by Shadi Torbey, published by Z-Man Games) — Part of the Oniverse series, you’re racing your submarine to the Abyss, lair of the Darkhouse, before the Phantom Submarine reaches your homeland, the Happy Island. It’s a dice game where you move and recruit crew at the same time, and the way hiring works (adjacent placements after your first crew member) is clever. I love the strategy and the feel of moving the submarines, usually I’d play it more than once in a sitting, but didn’t have time this month. Great for people who like to chill with dice and a quick game. 8/10.

The Lost Expedition (designed by Peer Sylvester, published by Osprey Games) — A team of three explorers trying to reach a lost city through the jungle. It’s a card game played across two phases, day and night. During the day, three cards come from the deck and you pick three more from your hand of six, then place all six in ascending order before resolving them left to right. At night, cards are placed one by one, and for each one you choose whether it goes on the left or right side, again three from the deck and three from your hand, resolved the same way, left to right. Along the way you’ll face all kinds of dangers from the jungle: animals, indigenous peoples, attacks, and you’ll have to survive using your wits. I really enjoy this game even though I’ve lost most of my attempts. It’s wonderfully thematic, you can build a whole story out of how the cards resolve. 8/10.

ROVE (designed by Dustin Dobson and Milan Zivkovic, published by Button Shy Games) — A micro-game of just 18 cards, a puzzle where you move cards under certain conditions to solve 7 patterns and win. It sounds simple, but managing your action points wisely, and picking patterns that unlock more actions, makes it clever. My two plays this month were with a wrong rule though, I only allowed moves of one space, which made the game much harder than it should be, so of course I lost miserably both times! Only 15 minutes to play, and it comes in a wonderfully compact format, perfect for travel. 8.5/10.

SOS Titanic (designed by Bruno Cathala and Ludovic Maublanc, published by TGG Games) — A solitaire-style game where your goal is to save the Titanic’s passengers as you turn the pages of a book showing the ship sinking. Save everyone and you win, otherwise you lose. I’ve played it 5 times and never won! I am really bad at this game. The game is simple at its core, but the iconography on some cards is genuinely hard to parse, I’d have preferred the action descriptions written directly on the cards instead of constantly checking the rulebook, which takes away from the enjoyment. I don’t dislike it, but I don’t love it either. 6/10, the challenge is there, but having to keep the rulebook in hand is annoying.

Demeter (designed by Matthieu Verdier, published by Sorry We Are French) — In Demeter you’re discovering and studying dinosaurs on a distant moon. It’s a flip-and-write game where you choose from four available actions, and by chaining them together you can pull off some really satisfying combo sequences. No two plays feel quite the same, since the objectives are randomly drafted each game. The theme comes through nicely, and the paper design is lovely. I’ve only played it solo, and since it’s a beat-your-own-score (BYOS) game with nothing to tell you whether your score is actually good or not, I don’t think it suits solo play. You only really notice this at the end, though, during the game itself it feels just as engaging as it would with others at the table. I’d give it 6/10 for solo, it’ll most likely shine more in multiplayer.

Trek12: Himalaya (designed by Bruno Cathala and Corentin Lebrat, published by Lumberjacks Studio) — A roll-and-write where you’re part of an expedition scaling the Himalayas, trying to score the highest to win. Each turn you roll two dice and choose from several mathematical operations, sum, subtract, multiply, or keep the higher or lower value, to decide which number to place next. At the end you score for each cordée (a sequence of consecutive numbers, you can build several, each one scoring individually with a bonus for the longest) and for zones of matching numbers, scored the same way, individually, with a bonus for the biggest. In solo mode you play against an automa that always places its number in the same spot as yours and always picks the higher option. The game is engaging, and comes with several mountains and sealed envelopes to open once you reach certain milestones. I like it enough to play it every week without getting bored. I will rate it 7/10.

Harmonies (designed by Johan Benvenuto, published by Libellud) — This time I played at 4 players, a change from the two-player games I covered in my full review here. I’m a huge fan of this game, the artwork is gorgeous, and that quiet, puzzly satisfaction I described in the review holds up just as well with a full table. I’m always up for another round.

Looking Ahead

For July, I’m hoping to get Black Rose Wars to the table, keep progressing through the It’s a Wonderful World campaign, and play an escape-game style experience with 50 Clues.

What About You?

And you, what did you play this month? I’d love to hear your thoughts! Come find me on Mastodon and Facebook.

item.title: Legacy of Yu – A Race Against the Flood
item.description:
Hello everyone!

Today we are travelling to ancient China to help Yu build canals and hold back the relentless floods of the Yellow River. This is Legacy of Yu, a solo campaign game that kept me on the edge of my seat through twelve plays and counting.

Game Overview

Legacy of Yu is a 2023 release for one player, ages 12+, with a playtime of around 60 minutes. It was designed by Shem Phillips, illustrated by Sam Phillips, and published by Garphill Games. I own the French edition, published by Pixie Games.

The game won the Best Solo Game of 2023 awards from the Dice Tower, BoardGameGeek (Golden Geek Award), and the Origins Game Fair.

Theme

During the reign of Emperor Yao, the people of ancient China lived under the constant threat of floods from the Yellow River. To put an end to the devastation, Yao appointed Gun, one of his officials, to find a solution. After nine years of failed attempts, Gun was gone, and his son Yu inherited the task. Rather than following his father’s approach of dams and dikes, Yu devised something different: a network of canals to redirect the floodwaters into nearby fields and smaller waterways.

That is the role you step into. You are Yu, and it is on you to build those canals, protect your village from barbarian raids, and keep the flood at bay, one round at a time.

How to Win

Legacy of Yu is a fully resettable, nonlinear campaign. The campaign ends after seven wins or seven losses, whichever comes first.

To win a single game, you need to complete all six canal sections and survive to the end of that round. There are three ways to lose: the Flood moves onto an unbuilt canal section (or off the right edge of the board); the Barbarians reach seven cards above the board; or you need to destroy a Townsfolk Card but have none left.

The campaign never locks you out. A loss gives you a bonus card to help in the next game, and a win lets you unlock new story content and move the campaign forward. Either way, you keep playing.

Gameplay

Each game has no fixed number of rounds. Instead, the Flood advances every time your Ready Pile runs out and you need to shuffle your Exhausted Pile to form a new one. That is the ticking clock at the heart of the game: the more cards you cycle through, the closer the Flood creeps.

At the start of each round you draw Townsfolk Cards from your Ready Pile and collect workers and resources during the Harvest phase. Resources come in several forms: cowrie shells, wood, clay, and provisions. Workers come in five types: Labourers (white), Fighters (red), Riders (black), Spearmen (blue), and Archers (yellow).

During the Take Actions phase, you use your Townsfolk Cards and spend resources and workers to act. You can build canal sections, fight barbarians, recruit new Townsfolk, and construct buildings. Each of those choices costs resources, and resources are never quite enough.

Townsfolk Cards have two uses. You can play them for their immediate resource effect and move them to your Exhausted Pile, or you can tuck them under the board to activate a permanent ability that triggers every Harvest. Those tuck spaces are unlocked by constructing Huts, and only one space is available at the start of the game.

Building a canal section costs the workers and cowrie shells shown on the Canal Card. You can only build once per round, and each section you complete unlocks new build sites along the river.

Fighting barbarians costs the provisions shown on the board below their card, plus the workers shown on the card itself. Any barbarian you do not defeat during your turn triggers the Suffer Attacks phase at the end of the round: each remaining barbarian either forces you to destroy a Townsfolk Card from your Ready Pile, or you can pay a bribe in workers or resources to avoid the damage. Leaving barbarians alone is never truly safe, and if you ever have seven of them above the board, you lose immediately.

The campaign storybook also triggers at certain moments, unlocking paragraphs that can be good or bad. I will not spoil those discoveries here.

Components

The box comes with a well-designed insert that organises all resources neatly and doubles as storage during play. Setup is quick because everything has its place, and cleanup is even quicker. The cards feel solid, the meeples are satisfying to handle, and the cardboard tokens have a good weight and finish. Honestly, I wish more games shipped with inserts this thoughtful.

My Experience

I have played Legacy of Yu around twelve times across two restarts, but I have never actually finished a campaign yet. My last run stands at five wins and two losses, and I am close to the end this time. I restarted twice after leaving the game untouched for a while, and each time it pulled me right back in.

The tension in this game is real. You are constantly juggling resources between building canals, fighting barbarians, and investing in your engine, and the puzzle never quite resolves cleanly. Every time I think I have a good plan, something disrupts it, and I have to adapt.

I have to share my favourite moment from one of my plays. I was sailing through a game feeling unusually confident, everything running smoothly. Almost at the finish line, I realised I had completely forgotten to pay provisions when fighting barbarians. I had been defeating them in a row like some kind of unstoppable hero. Lesson learned: when Legacy of Yu feels too easy, you are almost certainly doing something wrong. 😅

The final canal sections are the hardest to build. They require more resources at exactly the moment when you also have more barbarians to deal with. That last stretch is where games are won and lost.

My Rating

Note: 8/10

I love this game and would happily play it many times in a row. The campaign is beautifully designed, the insert is a dream, and the tension rarely lets up. The only real downside is that a bad barbarian card at the start can feel punishing before your engine is running. Some barbarians, especially further into the campaign, require a lot of resources to defeat, and if you draw one early with very little built, it can be discouraging. It does not ruin the experience, but it is worth knowing going in.

Final Thoughts

Legacy of Yu earns its awards, and it does so by doing something deceptively simple: it makes every single game feel tight. You are never comfortably ahead. There is always one more barbarian to deal with, one more resource you are short of, one more round where everything could unravel. If you enjoy solo games that keep you thinking until the very last action, this one is for you. If you prefer a more relaxed experience where you can build up and cruise to victory, it will probably frustrate you. But if you are the kind of player who grins when a plan barely comes together, Legacy of Yu will have you setting it up again before you have even put the pieces away.

Your Turn

Have you played Legacy of Yu? I would love to know how your campaign went, and whether you ever caught yourself playing a rule wrong and sailing through the game a little too smoothly. Come share them on Mastodon and Facebook.

item.title: It's a Wonderful World, and a Wonderful Game
item.description:
Hello everyone!

Today I want to share with you a game that I love and play a lot: It’s a Wonderful World. This is a game of hand management, set collection, and engine building, where you will develop your empire to be better than your competitors.

Game Overview

It’s a Wonderful World is a 2019 release for 1 to 5 players, ages 14+, with a playtime of 45 minutes. It was designed by Frédéric Guérard and illustrated by Anthony Wolff and published by La Boîte de Jeu & Origames.

Theme

In It’s a Wonderful World, you are the leader of an expanding empire. You will carefully plan your expansion by developing your resource production in order to rule over the world.

Gameplay

A game of It’s a Wonderful World is made up of 4 rounds, and each round has a draft phase, a planning phase, and a production phase.

During the draft phase, each player takes 7 cards, chooses one, and passes the deck to the right or left depending on the round. At 2 players, the draft works differently: each player starts with 10 cards instead of 7, choosing one at a time and passing the rest to the other player. When each player has 3 cards remaining, those are discarded without gaining their recycling bonus. This way, both players still end the draft phase with 7 cards.

During the planning phase, each player selects which cards go into production and which will be recycled. Each card has a resource associated with it. When you recycle a card, you gain that resource and place it on a card in production. If you’re not able to or don’t want to, you place the cube on your empire card instead. For every 5 resources, regardless of type, you can exchange them for a Krystallium, a bonus resource that can replace any other resource and be used at any time. Note that, if recycling a card during the planning phase places the final resource on a card under construction, that card is immediately completed and moves to your empire, already able to produce resources in that same round.

During the production phase, starting from the materials resource on the leftmost side, each player checks how many resources their empire produces. For each resource, the empire that produces the most earns the supremacy bonus, which is a general or a financier token. If there’s a tie, no one gets the bonus for that resource. Each player then takes the cubes produced and places them on the cards in production. As soon as a card finishes being constructed, it immediately moves to your empire and starts producing right away, following the normal production order. Resources that have already been produced earlier in this phase aren’t produced again for that newly completed card.

How to Win

The player with the most points at the end of the game wins. Points can come directly from cards or through multipliers that give points based on your production types and your generals/financiers.

Components

I own the Kickstarter version of the game, the Heritage box. This box brings an insert system that is just fantastic. The game also included the two campaign boxes, War or Peace and Leisure and Decadence. Later I also backed the Corruption and Ascension expansion, which fits perfectly into the box. For the insert, I’ll rate it 10/10.

Resources are represented by grey cubes for materials, black cubes for energy, green cubes for science, yellow for gold, blue for exploration, and red for Krystallium. There are also tokens for generals and tokens for financiers.

The player boards are made of two parts that, when joined, form the shape of an arrow. This gives you a hint about the order of production.

One thing to keep in mind: Krystallium is incredibly useful during the game, but it is worthless at the end, so make sure you spend it before the final round is over!

Setup

The game is really quick to set up, mostly thanks to the wonderful insert. Each resource has its own little container that keeps the cubes neatly in place. In total, the game uses 8 different resources.

Solo Mode

In solo mode, the traditional draft isn’t possible, so the rules are adjusted.

When setting up, prepare 8 stacks of 5 cards. These will be your draft cards for the whole game. Each round, you select a stack and look at the cards. Choose the cards you want to produce. At any point, you also have the option to discard 2 cards to look at the top 5 cards of the deck and pick one to add to your hand. You can use this option as many times as you like. You then decide whether each card goes to production or recycling. Once you’ve decided what to do with every card, take a new stack and repeat the process.

After two stacks, you move to the production phase. The only real difference from multiplayer is the supremacy bonus: in solo mode, you earn it for a resource if you produce more than 5 cubes of it, rather than comparing against opponents. At the end of the game, compare your score to the performance chart: under 60 points is Rookie, 60+ is Dictator, 80+ is Emperor, and 100+ is Living God. If you’re playing a solo scenario, each one also has its own bronze, silver, and gold medal thresholds to aim for.

My Experience

This game completely conquered my heart. The theme isn’t very present, but the satisfaction of choosing which cards to construct, and arriving at the 4th round able to construct everything, is wonderful. The rules are simple to understand and easy to remember too. I went a full year without playing, and after putting it back on the table, I quickly remembered all the rules. The rulebook is well written, with plenty of diagrams and images that help you grasp the rules.

My 2-player experience with just the base game was really good. I liked the draft phase and how it plays out. The fact that everyone plays simultaneously is also nice, as it makes the game shorter and avoids dead time between turns.

The game comes with solo scenarios that give you certain cards you must construct, plus a score to beat. Knowing your goals from the start is an advantage, since it helps you plan ahead, and at the end of the game it can be useful for deciding which point cards to prioritize.

My Rating

Note: 10/10

I never get bored with this game, and I’m always ready for one more play. I love everything about it, and it showed me that a theme doesn’t need to be front and center for a game to be great. In my May 2026 review I rated it 9/10, but after more thought, I realized the lighter theme genuinely doesn’t bother me.

Final Thoughts

It’s a Wonderful World has earned a permanent spot in my collection, and honestly, in my heart. The blend of drafting, hand management, and engine building creates a deeply satisfying puzzle every time I sit down with it, and the fact that it works so well solo, at two players, or with a full table makes it incredibly versatile. If you haven’t tried it yet, I can’t recommend it enough. And if you have the chance to grab the Heritage edition with its insert, do it, your future self will thank you. I’m currently deep into the Leisure & Decadence expansion, so expect more from this game soon!

Your Turn

Have you played It’s a Wonderful World, solo or with others? What do you enjoy most about it, and is there anything that doesn’t quite work for you? I’d love to hear your thoughts! Come share them on Mastodon and Facebook.

item.title: May 2026 Plays
item.description:
Hello everyone!

May was a quieter month than April, at least by the numbers, but no less enjoyable. I revisited some firm favourites, discovered a few charming new games, and had a great time around the table with others. I have to admit, Minos, Unconscious Mind, and Luthier, which I was hoping to finally get to the table, once again didn’t make it. Lack of time got in the way, but they will soon. Let’s get into it!

May 2026 by the Numbers

  • 24 plays (vs. 32 in April)
  • 11 different games
  • 5 new-to-me games
  • Most played: Ancient Knowledge and It’s a Wonderful World

It’s a Wonderful World — My Favourite of the Month

Sometimes I ask myself why I love this game so much. And then I play it, and the answer becomes obvious: there is nothing quite like the satisfaction of constructing every single card by the end of the fourth round, watching your empire hum along exactly as planned.

The design is really clever. You’re building cards that allow your empire to produce goods and score points, but the order in which you construct them matters. A card built early can start producing in that same round, as long as the relevant good hasn’t been produced yet. Goods are generated in a fixed order, so planning your sequence well is what separates a smooth engine from a frustrated one. That puzzle is exactly what I love about this game.

I’ve played the War or Peace campaign both solo and at two players, and now I’m starting Leisure and Decadence for the first time, playing solo. The campaigns bring new mechanics that make the game really shine, and they do it all behind a story that is genuinely well constructed. I also always play with the Corruption and Ascension expansion. It can help or hurt depending on how you build your strategy: some of those cards are really worth constructing, but they demand a lot of resources. Will you be patient enough to pull it off?

My rating: 9/10. The only thing holding it back is that the theme doesn’t always feel fully present during play. But the puzzle and the engine more than make up for it. If you enjoy engine building and don’t need a game to be heavily thematic, I fully recommend this one.

Ancient Knowledge

I already have a full review of Ancient Knowledge on the blog, so I won’t go into detail here. The short version: you’re the architect of ancient wonders, and the real heart of the game is deciding when to spend your cards and how to manage where they enter the timeline. Should you push a monument closer to the past, or keep it in play a little longer? That tension is what makes the game tick.

I’ll be honest, the theme doesn’t feel fully present after a while. But the enjoyment of managing what to play and when is real, and I genuinely love watching the monuments drift toward the past. It took me several plays to really get into it, and I’ve only played solo so far. Worth the patience.

My rating: 8/10 — same as in the review. A game that rewards patience and grows on you with every play.

Fromage and Fromaggio

These two are standalone games that can also be combined as expansions of each other. I’ve now played Fromage at three players and solo, and Fromaggio solo. I haven’t mixed them yet, but I’m curious to try.

My verdict? I really like this game. As someone pointed out during my three-player session, the first play can feel a little overwhelming. There’s a lot to track: plate colours, cheese colours, the different scoring conditions for each location, plus cows, buildings, and fruits. But after that first play, everything clicks into place and you start to see the strategies.

If you ask me which one I prefer, honestly, I can’t say. Both are really good. But they’re also quite similar, so there’s nothing dramatically new if you own both. My recommendation: start with Fromage. After several plays, if you’re still hooked and want a bit more variety, then pick up Fromaggio. No need to rush into both at once. The components are fantastic, by the way, in both the retail and premium versions.

My rating: 8/10 for both. Funny, addictive, and very well made.

Time Bomb

Time Bomb is a party game that plays quickly and will almost certainly make you laugh. We played at five players, and it wasn’t my first time with it. Every time I play, I enjoy it just as much as the first.

The idea is simple and brilliant. Each player receives a set of face-down cards showing parts of a bomb. Some cables can be cut to defuse it, others do nothing, and somewhere in the deck is the bomb itself. Players look at their own cards, shuffle them, and lay them face-down in front of them. The first player then cuts a cable by flipping one of another player’s cards. That player becomes the next to cut, and so the game goes, one cable at a time. Two hidden teams are at play throughout: Sherlock’s side is trying to defuse the bomb, Moriarty’s side is trying to make it explode. And here’s the funny part: after your very first play, you’ll never quite trust what anyone tells you again. Everyone claims to have the right cables in front of them. Everyone.

My rating: 8/10. If you enjoy bluffing games and hidden traitor mechanics, this one belongs in your collection.

Other Notable Games

Broom Service

One play at four players, and I had a brilliant time. The theme is charming: you run a delivery service for witches, collecting ingredients and fulfilling orders across a magical realm. The core mechanic is wonderfully tense: you play a card and declare whether you want to be brave or cowardly. The brave action is stronger, but if another player plays the same card and also chooses brave, they can steal the action from you. Reading what other players might do, second-guessing their choices, deciding whether to play it safe or go for it — it’s all very funny and surprisingly interactive.

I enjoyed the game and the mechanisms a lot, but I’d need more plays before giving it a proper rating. For now, 7/10, with the caveat that it might go higher. If someone invites me to play this again, I’ll say yes immediately.

Onirim

I already have a full review on the blog. Onirim is a game I love, and it reminds me of classic solitaire card games. Fair warning: if you’re not a fan of shuffling, this one might test your patience. You’ll be doing it often. Absolutely worth it.

My rating: 8/10 — as in the review. A perfect everyday game that never overstays its welcome.

Codenames

Codenames is fun, but it really depends on the group. 6/10 from me. The game itself is sharp and clever, and you can see how much better players get together over time. But if someone at the table struggles with word associations or is a bit more reserved, it can become a painful experience rather than an enjoyable one. Sweet spot for me is around six players.

Age of Civilization

I had only played this one solo before, so this month I tried it at two players for the first time. It’s a pleasant little game built around timing: actions move through the eras, so things that are useful early may not be available late, and vice versa. I still feel like I need more plays to really get comfortable with it. For now, 6/10. Quick, easy to play, perfectly fine. I’d play again, but it wouldn’t be my first pick off the shelf.

Suburbia

My first solo play, and I have mixed feelings. The city-building puzzle is genuinely enjoyable: managing your borough, deciding what to build next, balancing income and growth. But the rules are messy and hard to follow, and the player aid offers no clear ordering of the tiles, which makes looking things up frustrating. 6/10 for now, but I need more plays before saying anything definitive. The potential is there.

Ohio Bob

One play, and a win. It’s a small, clever little game you can take anywhere. The rules are a touch unclear in places — I had to check the FAQ to sort out a couple of doubts — but nothing that broke the experience. 7/10 so far, and I’ll definitely be going back to try harder levels.

Looking Ahead

June is looking promising! I’m planning my first plays of Minos and Unconscious Mind, two games I’m really curious about. Septima already had one play and left me wanting more, so it’s definitely coming back to the table. And Hogwarts Battle… it’s a game I love and have been missing, so it’s time to give it the attention it deserves. I hope it will be a great month!

What About You?

May had a nice mix of familiar favourites and new discoveries. It’s a Wonderful World continues to be one of those games I simply can’t put down, and Fromage turned out to be a real treat. Have you played any of these? I’d love to hear your thoughts! Come find me on Mastodon and Facebook.

item.title: Onirim – Lost in the Labyrinth of Dreams
item.description:
Hello everyone!

Today I’m taking you on a journey through the world of dreams. Will you find all the doors and escape the labyrinth before the nightmares consume you? Let me show you how it works.

Table of Contents
  • Game Overview
  • Theme
  • How to Win
  • Key Concepts
  • Gameplay
  • Setup & Components
  • The Little Incubus
  • The Expansions
    • The Book of Steps Lost and Found
    • The Glyphs
    • The Dreamcatchers
    • The Towers
    • Happy Dreams and Dark Premonitions
    • Crossroads and Dead Ends
    • The Door to the Oniverse
  • My Experience
  • My Rating
  • Final Thoughts
  • Your Turn

Game Overview

Onirim is a 2014 release for 1–2 players, ages 10+, with a playtime of 15 minutes. It was designed by Shadi Torbey and illustrated by Élise Plessis. Onirim was originally published by Z-Man Games. The English edition is now published directly by inPatience.

The second edition includes the base game plus all seven expansions in one box. It was also nominated for the 2014 Golden Geek Best Solo Board Game award.

Theme

You are a Dreamwalker, lost in the labyrinth of dreams. To find your way out, you must discover the eight Onirim doors hidden somewhere in the deck. But your path is not clear: nightmares lurk among the cards, ready to disrupt your plans and make your escape all the harder.

The entire game is played with a single deck of cards, made up of location cards, door cards, and nightmare cards. Simple, elegant, and surprisingly tense.

How to Win

You win by finding and unlocking all eight doors before the deck runs out. Doors can be claimed in two ways: by playing a sequence of three cards of the same colour with no repeated symbols in your labyrinth row, or by discarding a key card from your hand when a door is drawn. Run out of cards before you find them all, and you lose.

Key Concepts

A few terms come up throughout the game and are worth knowing before diving into gameplay:

Limbo is a temporary holding area. Nightmare and door cards that cannot be immediately resolved go here, and are shuffled back into the deck at specific moments during the game.

Card types in the deck are:

  • Sun and moon cards: standard location cards with no special effects, used to build your labyrinth row.
  • Key cards: can be played like sun or moon cards, but also have a special power. Discarding a key triggers a prophecy: look at the top five cards of the deck, discard one, then arrange the remaining four in any order and return them to the top.

Gameplay

I will describe the solo rules, as that is the only way I have played.

On each turn you play or discard a card from your hand, then draw back up to five cards. Cards are played into your labyrinth row, and the rule is simple but strict: you cannot repeat a symbol consecutively. So if your last card was a sun, the next one must be a moon or a key.

Each time you draw, there is a chance the new card is a nightmare. When that happens, you must resolve it immediately using one of four options:

  • Discard a key card from your hand
  • Send one of your already-claimed door cards back to limbo
  • Reveal and discard the top five cards of the deck (doors and nightmares among them go to limbo instead)
  • Discard your entire hand, then redraw as at setup (any doors or nightmares in the new draw go to limbo)

The tension of these decisions is where most of the game lives.

Setup & Components

Inside the box you will find a fold-out insert that holds all the cards perfectly. The little Incubus token sits in there too, a small but beautifully crafted pawn. The card illustrations are immersive and atmospheric, and the overall material quality is excellent.

Setup is refreshingly quick. Shuffle the full deck (base game only to start), draw five cards as your opening hand. Any doors or nightmares in that initial hand go to limbo, and you keep drawing until you have five valid cards. Shuffle limbo back into the deck and you are ready to go. Even when adding expansions, setup rarely takes more than a couple of extra minutes.

The rulebook is short and well-written, with clear illustrations that make the rules easy to grasp even for first-time players.

The Little Incubus

The Little Incubus is a token included in the base game that offers three difficulty levels.

Easy mode: Once per game, you can cancel the effect of a nightmare card by discarding the Incubus token.

Normal mode: The Incubus lets you anticipate a nightmare. At any point, you can place the Incubus on the next card you will draw. If that card is a location or door card, tuck it under the Incubus. Later, when you actually draw a nightmare, you can discard that tucked card instead, treating it as if you had already resolved the nightmare earlier. Once used, the Incubus is available again.

Hard mode: Works the same as normal mode, but you must tuck two cards under the Incubus instead of one, raising the cost of the protection.

The Expansions

The second edition comes with seven expansions, each designed to be played individually or combined. I have played each one separately but have not yet mixed them. Below is a section for each one, followed by my overall thoughts. One thing worth mentioning: each expansion includes the necessary material to be combined with the others, and some even have specific integration rules. For example, the four extra door cards from The Glyphs are designed to be incorporated into The Book of Steps Lost and Found when playing both together. Each expansion is also easily identifiable by a unique symbol printed on the lower right corner of its cards, which makes sorting and setting up any combination quick and painless.

The Book of Steps Lost and Found

This expansion adds a new victory condition on top of finding the doors: you must unlock them in a specific order. At the start of the game, shuffle the eight goal cards and reveal them in a row. That sequence is your target.

To compensate for the added difficulty, the expansion introduces spells. These are powerful actions triggered by removing cards from the discard pile. Depending on which spell you cast, you can perform a prophecy, swap two goal cards in the sequence, or discard a nightmare outright. The strategic layer this adds is genuinely satisfying. It does not increase the game length much, but it meaningfully deepens the experience.

The Glyphs

This module introduces 12 new cards: eight glyph cards (two of each colour) and four additional door cards, bringing the total doors you need to find from eight to twelve.

Glyph cards work similarly to key cards. Discarding one lets you look at the top five cards of the deck: if a door is among them, claim it immediately, then place the rest at the bottom. If there is no door, all five go to the bottom. The new glyph symbol also adds a fourth option to your labyrinth row, giving you more flexibility when building sequences.

The difficulty increase from finding twelve doors instead of eight is real, but well-balanced by the new power. A worthy addition.

The Dreamcatchers

This expansion adds ten new cards: four lost dream cards, four dreamcatcher cards, and two fail-safe book cards. It also adds a second goal alongside finding the doors: you must catch all the lost dream cards before the game ends.

Lost dream cards behave like doors and go to limbo when drawn. But here is the twist: limbo is no longer automatically reshuffled into the deck. Instead, to move limbo cards onto a dreamcatcher (catching them), you need a freeing. Freeing happens automatically whenever an effect would shuffle limbo back (for example, during a prophecy), or you can trigger one manually by discarding a fail-safe book card. Only two of those are available, so they are precious.

If you have limbo cards but no available dreamcatcher to receive them, you suffer an overload and lose one dreamcatcher. Managing that tension, deciding when to force a freeing and when to push your luck, is what makes this expansion tick. A clever and fun module.

The Towers

This expansion adds 12 tower cards (three of each colour), shuffled into the deck. It introduces a third victory condition: by the end of the game, you must also have built a defence line of four tower cards showing all four different colours.

Tower cards cannot be added to your labyrinth row. Instead, you place them into the defence line directly from your hand. But there is a catch: each time a nightmare is triggered, you must discard one tower from the defence line unless you resolve the nightmare by reshuffling it back into the deck rather than discarding it. Once all four colours are in place and the line is complete, nightmares no longer affect it.

Tower cards also have an active power: discard one from your hand to look at the top three, four, or five cards of the deck (depending on the number printed on the card), then rearrange them in any order you choose.

I read the rules and thought this would make things easier. I was wrong. It makes the decisions harder and the game more demanding. I loved it.

Happy Dreams and Dark Premonitions

This expansion adds four happy dream cards (shuffled into the deck) and eight dark premonition cards. At setup, shuffle the premonitions and reveal four face-up on the table. The remaining four form a face-down draw pile next to them.

The dark premonitions are condition cards. Each one states a specific condition, and the moment that condition is met during the game, you must resolve its penalty immediately. If multiple premonitions trigger at the same time, you choose the resolution order. If resolving one means another’s condition is no longer met, skip the second.

The penalties are punishing and all tied to the doors you unlock. One might tell you that as soon as you find two doors of the same colour, you must send one of them back to limbo. Another forces you to discard all red cards from your hand the moment you claim both red doors. A third makes you reshuffle a nightmare back into the deck. Managing the order in which you unlock doors becomes a real strategic consideration.

Happy dream cards are the counterbalance. When drawn, resolve one immediately: either discard the top dark premonition from the draw pile (removing a future threat), or take the top seven cards of the deck, discard as many as you like, and return the rest in any order. Powerful, but watch out: one premonition specifically punishes you for finding happy dreams, so be careful how you sequence your door unlocks.

A real challenge, and one of the more strategically rich expansions.

Crossroads and Dead Ends

This expansion adds six crossroad cards and ten dead end cards, all shuffled into the deck.

Crossroad cards are jokers: they count as any colour, making it easier to complete sequences in your labyrinth row. Dead end cards are the opposite. They land in your hand like normal cards but cannot be played or discarded as a dream card, taking up space and reducing your options with every turn.

The dead ends can be a real pain. You end up almost wishing for a nightmare just to have a reason to discard your whole hand and start fresh. There is actually an escape action that lets you do exactly that, but the catch is that it does not resolve the nightmare: you discard your hand, draw five new cards, and the nightmare is still there waiting for you. So in my opinion the better play is to just wait for a real nightmare and use it to your advantage.

I enjoyed this one even though I lost my first game with it. It is lighter than some of the other expansions, offering a small but welcome help with the crossroads while adding a new and rather sneaky kind of pressure with the dead ends.

The Door to the Oniverse

This expansion includes 16 denizen cards, from which you randomly select 8 at setup. The remaining 8 are set aside unseen. The selected denizens are shuffled into the deck along with one new multicolour door, which can be claimed by a sequence of any colour and counts toward your win condition.

When you draw a denizen card, you make a choice: keep it or discard it. Kept denizens do not count toward your hand size and accumulate without limit. To keep one, though, you must discard a dream card from your hand, which means drawing two new cards to refill, and that raises your nightmare risk considerably. At any point you can discard a kept denizen to activate its effect. Powers include playing a card that matches the last symbol in your labyrinth row (bypassing the no-repeat rule), or swapping a card from your hand with one from the discard pile.

I thought this would ease the game. It does not. It makes it more strategic, and the question of whether to purchase a denizen and accept the risk is consistently interesting.

My Experience

I have played Onirim more than 40 times and I genuinely cannot say I am tired of it. There is something almost hypnotic about it, a quality very similar to playing Solitaire on a computer: quick to set up, easy to pick up, and yet there is always one more game to play.

That comparison is not random. Onirim genuinely reminds me of the hours I spent playing Solitaire as a kid, and I think that nostalgia plays a real role in why I fell so hard for this game.

But beyond the nostalgia, the game has real tension. Every card drawn creates a small moment of dread. When I am one sequence away from a door and I draw a nightmare, the decision of what to sacrifice is never easy. I have never once sent a door back to limbo: losing a door feels too costly, and I always try to find another way. A key in hand feels like a lifeline. Drawing a nightmare, discarding it with a key, and then immediately drawing another one is a special kind of frustration. And then the question: discard the top five cards of the deck, or sacrifice my whole hand? Discarding from the deck means losing cards I did not choose, possibly precious keys. Discarding my hand means rebuilding from scratch.

Those decisions are why I keep coming back.

If I had to rank the expansions today:

  1. The Book of Steps Lost and Found
  2. The Towers
  3. The Glyphs
  4. Happy Dreams and Dark Premonitions
  5. The Door to the Oniverse
  6. The Dreamcatchers
  7. Crossroads and Dead Ends

But this ranking will probably shift the more I play. There is genuinely no expansion here I dislike.

What I can say is that I now add an expansion every single time I play. They are easy to understand and integrate, so there is no barrier to just picking one and adding it in. And having seven expansions in the same box is just great, you always have something different to try without having to buy more stuff. This gives the game so much life and so many hours ahead.

It is also worth noting: this is my go-to travel game. The box is perfectly sized, there are no pieces to lose, and you can have a full game in 15 minutes. So far only Nautilion comes close for quick play, but it has too many pieces to be practical on the go. Onirim holds that crown for now.

My Rating

Note: 8/10

Onirim is a perfect everyday game. It captures the same satisfying, slightly addictive quality of Solitaire: quick to set up, easy to learn, and hard to put down. The box is just the right size, the material quality is excellent, and I have a particular soft spot for the fold-out insert and the little Incubus token.

If you enjoy puzzles and short plays on a busy or tiring day, this game is for you. If you prefer games with strong storytelling or a rich thematic presence, it may not be what you are looking for. But if you ever loved Solitaire, I can almost guarantee you will love this too. With seven expansions in the box, there is plenty to keep you busy for a long time.

Final Thoughts

Onirim has earned a permanent place in my collection and in my heart. It is simple, tense, beautifully made, and endlessly replayable. Each expansion adds a new dimension without ever overcomplicating what makes the base game so satisfying.

I will absolutely be reviewing the other games in the Oniverse series, and playing through them for those posts will be a great excuse to spend more time with each one. Nautilion is already waiting.

Your Turn

Have you played Onirim? Do you play the base game, or do you mix in the expansions? And if you do combine them, which ones are your favourites together? I would love to hear how your experiences compare to mine! Come share your thoughts on Mastodon and Facebook.

item.title: Ancient Knowledge – Will Your Monuments Stand the Test of Time?
item.description:
Hello everyone!

Today I am taking you on a journey through the ancient world with Ancient Knowledge, a game that will test your ability to build, plan, and let go, because time waits for no one.

Game Overview

Ancient Knowledge is a 2023 release for 2 to 4 players, ages 12+, with a playtime of 30 minutes per player. It was designed by Rémi Mathieu, illustrated by Emilien Rotival, Adrien Rives, and Pierre Ples, and published by Iello. I own and played the French edition, also published by Iello.

The Heritage expansion, released in 2024, adds a solo mode in two variants as well as new Builder and Technology cards that enrich the base game for all player counts.

Theme

You are the last heirs of a great ancient civilisation. Your role is to preserve the knowledge of your people and ensure it survives the passage of time. Monuments rise and fall: pyramids, megaliths, cities, all the great constructions of the ancient world appear on the cards, from the Sphinx of Giza to the temples of Tiwanaku. But nothing lasts forever. Everything you build will eventually slide into the past, and the knowledge attached to it will be lost unless you act in time.

How to Win

The player with the most victory points at the end of the game wins. Points come from the monuments themselves, from certain card effects that score at the end, and from your Level II Technology cards. The game ends when one player accumulates 14 or more monuments in their Past, at which point the current round is completed and scores are counted. Lost knowledge tokens, those you failed to collect before a monument declined, subtract points from your final score.

Gameplay

Each turn has three phases. In the Action Phase, you take two actions chosen from five options: Create (play a monument or artifact card), Learn (take a Technology card from the central display), Archive (discard cards from your hand to remove knowledge tokens from monuments in your Timeline), Excavate (rotate monuments in your Past to draw cards), or Search (draw a single card). You can take the same action twice.

The core mechanic is the Timeline. When you create a monument, you place it in one of the six spaces above your board, based on the position shown on the card. Each space holds up to two monuments. Knowledge tokens are placed on each monument when it is created, representing the knowledge you can potentially collect. Every monument also has effects: some trigger immediately on creation, some activate each Timeline Phase, some trigger when declining, and some score at the end of the game.

At the end of each turn, during the Decline Phase, all your monuments slide one space to the left. When a monument reaches the first space, it goes into your Past. Any knowledge tokens still on it at that moment become lost knowledge, which costs you points at the end of the game.

You can pay extra cards from your hand to place a monument on a different space than the one printed on the card, closer to or further from the Past. I noticed this rule early on, but it took me a while to truly understand its importance, and more on that in My Experience.

Technology cards represent famous historical figures and advances. Level I cards have immediate or ongoing effects; Level II cards provide end-game points. Collecting them based on your monument types is a key part of building a strong engine.

Setup & Components

Setup is straightforward. Each player takes a Builder board, draws a starting hand, and the Technology tiles are laid out in the centre of the table with cards on each level. The box comes with a well-designed insert that fits the Heritage expansion material and has room for sleeved cards if you want to protect them. The card stock is excellent quality. The knowledge tokens are good but feel a little small in the hand. The first player token is a nice thematic touch, though I have to say I wished it were a little sculpt rather than a 3D cardboard piece. A missed opportunity!

Solo Mode

The solo mode requires the Heritage expansion. It offers two variants: Challenge Mode and Heritage Mode.

In Challenge Mode, you pick one of ten predefined challenges, each with a specific combination of objective cards to fulfil. I only tested the first challenge, but there are no persistent consequences between games, making it a great option for a one-off session.

Heritage Mode is a campaign. The goal is to complete all 15 objective cards across a series of games. At the start of your first Heritage game, you shuffle all 15 chest cards and draw 5. You then choose how many of those to take as objectives for this game, between 1 and 5. The more objectives you commit to, the fewer artifact spaces you have available during the game, since objectives occupy those same spaces on your board.

Each game lasts 16 turns, tracked by the Time card that slides through your Timeline and triggers the end of the game when it declines for the third time. A Technology Phase is added at the end of each turn: you roll the die, and the result removes one Technology card from the display, which adds real pressure to your planning.

If you fail to achieve all your chosen objectives, you lose and the campaign ends. If you succeed, the completed objective cards carry over to the next game, but flipped to show only their effect text. These unlocked events give you a one-time bonus during the following game, though any you do not use are discarded at the end.

Your score at the end of a winning game also shapes your next game. A high score means no penalty; a lower score means you start the next game with one or two fewer cards, or with the Time card placed closer to the edge, giving you fewer turns to accomplish your objectives.

My Experience

I have played Ancient Knowledge seven times solo, all using the Heritage expansion: my first five games in Challenge Mode and my last two in Heritage Mode.

My first few games were rough. I scored 38, then 41, lost twice without completing objectives, and at one point genuinely wondered if the game was for me. The rules are simple enough, but there are a lot of moving pieces, and the card interactions take time to absorb. Every time I came back after a break, I felt the same initial fog.

Then something clicked. I started to understand how to build combos: how to chain monument effects with the right Technology cards, how to time my Excavate actions to fuel my hand, how to balance immediate effects with end-game scoring. My scores started reflecting that: 48, then a best of 70, then 58 in my last Heritage session. I particularly enjoy the cards that let you draw more cards or remove knowledge tokens from monuments. They are powerful, and once you understand when to prioritise them, they make a real difference to your engine.

One specific thing that changed my game was learning to use the positional flexibility when creating monuments. You can discard extra cards from your hand to place a monument on a different space than the one printed on the card. For most of my early plays I knew this was possible but never used it intentionally. Once I started doing so, moving monuments closer or further based on what I needed, my planning improved dramatically.

The Heritage Mode added a new layer I did not expect to enjoy as much as I did. The weight of the campaign, knowing that a bad game ends your run, makes every decision feel meaningful. I am currently four objectives in and still going. And despite the pressure of objectives, I still enjoy the pure puzzle of optimising my engine within each game.

I have not tested the multiplayer mode yet, so I cannot speak to how player interaction plays out in practice. Looking at the cards, there does not seem to be a huge amount of direct interaction, but perhaps just enough to keep things interesting.

My Rating

Note: 8/10

Ancient Knowledge won me over gradually and honestly. The first plays are hard, the learning curve is real, and you will probably feel lost before you feel competent. But the satisfaction of finally building a smooth, comboing engine is genuinely rewarding. The Heritage Mode elevated the game further for me: the campaign structure gives it long-term purpose, and the tension of managing objectives while optimising your score is exactly the kind of solo puzzle I enjoy. The component quality is excellent, the design is elegant, and there is always more to discover.

Final Thoughts

If you enjoy engine-building card games and do not mind a learning curve, Ancient Knowledge is absolutely worth your time. Be patient with yourself in the first few games: it will feel slow and clunky before it feels smooth. Once it clicks, though, it really clicks. And if you play solo, do yourself a favour and pick up the Heritage expansion. It transforms the game from a series of individual puzzles into a proper campaign with stakes, and I think that is where Ancient Knowledge is at its best.

Your Turn

Ancient Knowledge is all about passing knowledge through time. How about you: have you played it? Are you working through the Heritage campaign, and how many objectives have you completed so far? Come share your thoughts on Mastodon and Facebook.
